How a CPU really works

Apple M5 Max · 6 performance + 12 efficiency cores · 128 GB unified · measured from scratch

A short course in what makes a processor fast or slow — taught entirely by measuring one. No spec sheets, no system call that hands you the answer. Just timed loops, a few honest tricks, and an explanation of what each number actually means.

The one rule of this course: separate what you measure from what you assume. The only things we ever truly measure are elapsed time and how many instructions we ran (we wrote them, so we know). Everything else — "GHz," "cycles," "instructions per cycle" — is those two divided, leaning on one stated assumption. Whenever an assumption can't be proven, the text says so. That's the line between measuring a machine and fooling yourself.

Chapter 1What is a clock cycle, and how fast does it tick?

A CPU has a heartbeat. A tiny crystal drives a clock signal that ticks billions of times a second, and the processor does its work on those ticks: each cycle is one tick. "4.5 GHz" just means 4.5 billion ticks per second. Almost everything about how fast a chip feels traces back to two numbers — how many ticks per second, and how much it gets done per tick.

So step one is to find the tick rate. You'd think you could just ask the operating system, but on Apple Silicon you can't: the true hardware cycle counter is privileged, off-limits to ordinary programs. So we have to measure it, with the trick the entire course is built on:

Build a chain of dependent additions — x = x+1; x = x+1; … — where each add needs the result of the one before it. The processor physically cannot start the next add until this one finishes, and a simple add finishes in exactly one tick. So the chain is forced to crawl forward at exactly one add per cycle. Count how many adds happen in a second, and that number is the cycles per second.

Run that and time it:

one dependent chain → ~4.57 billion adds / second two independent clocks (the OS timer and the chip's system timer) agree on the elapsed time to 0.00%

So we call it ~4.57 GHz — but be precise about what just happened. We measured two honest things: the time (with a stopwatch) and the number of adds (we wrote the loop, so we know it exactly). The jump to "GHz" assumes that one dependent add really does take exactly one cycle. We can't prove that from inside the program — but the answer lands right on Apple's published clock for these cores, which is strong corroboration. The fully honest label for our number is "billions of dependent adds per second," and we're choosing to call that GHz.

A nice gotcha: the chip actually has several clocks. That system timer we cross-checked against ticks at a steady 1 GHz, while the CPU core runs at ~4.5 GHz and constantly changes speed. A machine keeps a slow, rock-steady clock for telling time and a fast, variable one for doing work — and we've been measuring the second one through the first.

Chapter 2A single core does many things at once

Here's the fact that surprises almost everyone. Most people picture a CPU like this: read one instruction, do it, read the next, do it — a tidy single-file line. That mental model has been wrong for about thirty years. A modern core is superscalar: inside that one core are several separate execution units (multiple adders, and more), and in a single cycle it can fire off a whole handful of instructions at the same time.

We can prove it directly. Take our dependent chain from Chapter 1 — which is stuck at one add per cycle because each add waits for the last — and compare it to several chains that don't depend on each other. Same total number of adds, same one core:

adds completed per cycle, one core

1 dependent chain
1.0
8 independent
5.8

Almost 6× faster — same chip, same adds, same instant in time. The only thing that changed is whether the adds depended on each other. And that reveals the real reason the dependent chain was slow: not because adds are slow, but because each one had to wait for the previous result. Remove the waiting and the core's true width shows itself: it was capable of ~6 at once the whole time.

This is the first of two ideas that come back in every single chapter: independence is speed. Work that depends on previous work, step by step, can only go one-at-a-time no matter how powerful the hardware is. Work that's independent lets all that parallel machinery light up.

Chapter 3…but only if it can see the parallelism

If the core is ~6 wide, why did it manage only ~6 and not more — and why is squeezing that out finicky? Because of how the core finds independent work. It doesn't magically know which instructions are unrelated; it reads ahead in the instruction stream through a window of limited size, and from whatever it can see in that window, it picks out the ones whose inputs are ready and runs them together.

So where independent instructions sit in the stream matters. If you write each independent chain as one long contiguous block — 64 adds to a, then 64 to b, then 64 to c — the only independent work is dozens of instructions away, often past the edge of the window, and the extra execution units sit idle. If instead you interleave them — one add to a, one to b, one to c, repeat — the independent work is right next to each other and the core grabs it instantly. Identical arithmetic, just reordered:

same 8 independent chains, two orderings · adds/cycle

blocked
3.3
interleaved
5.8

Reordering the same instructions bought ~75% more throughput. This is not a trick — it's exactly why compilers spend real effort on instruction scheduling, shuffling independent operations close together so the core's out-of-order engine can actually exploit them. We just watched that optimization pay off by hand.

Chapter 4Now multiply by all the cores

Everything so far happened inside one core. This chip has 18 of them, and each can do all of the above independently. So the obvious question: does the work simply multiply by the number of cores? We run our wide loop on more and more threads at once and watch the total:

total integer throughput (billion/s) vs threads

It climbs nearly straight up to ~16 threads, and then hits a wall. Look at the end: 24 threads and 32 threads deliver the exact same 318 billion/second. That's not coincidence — there are only 18 cores, so once every core is busy, extra threads have nowhere to run and simply take turns. That flat line is the hardware's own core count, made visible by a stopwatch.

One honest wrinkle: the peak is ~15× a single core, not 18×. Two reasons. This chip has 6 fast "performance" cores and 12 slower "efficiency" cores, so they don't all contribute equally; and when every core is working the whole chip shares one power-and-heat budget, so the fast cores can't hold their top speed. 18 cores of hardware deliver about 15 cores of full-speed work. Expected, not a defect.

Chapter 5The memory wall

Every add so far used only registers — the tiny handful of storage slots built directly into the core, the fastest memory there is. Real programs can't fit in a handful of slots; they constantly reach out to main memory. And reaching into memory is where a fast core goes to wait.

To measure that wait with nothing else mixed in, we use a pointer chase: lay out a buffer so that each slot tells you which slot to read next, in a random order. Because each read's address comes from the previous read's result, the core can't run them in parallel or guess ahead — it must do them strictly one after another. That exposes the raw latency of a single memory access. Now grow the buffer and watch:

time for one dependent memory access vs buffer size · cycles

The latency doesn't rise smoothly — it climbs in cliffs. Each flat stretch is a different cache: a small, fast copy of memory kept close to the core. While your data fits in the nearest cache (L1) every access costs ~4 cycles; when it spills out, you drop to the next, larger, slower cache; and once it no longer fits in any cache you're talking to main memory (DRAM) at ~425 cycles — over 100× slower. We just drew the chip's entire memory hierarchy with nothing but timing.

Why does this dominate real performance? Put 425 cycles in perspective: in the time of one DRAM access, a core that can do ~6 instructions per cycle could have run about 2,500 instructions. Instead it's frozen, waiting for a single number to arrive. That's why real code rarely approaches the throughput ceilings from earlier chapters — it spends much of its life stalled on memory. Caches, and everything in the next chapter, exist to fight that stall.

Chapter 6Access pattern beats working-set size

The pointer chase was deliberately the worst case: random and dependent. Now change just one thing — make the accesses predictable. Walk the very same big buffer in order (slot 0, 1, 2, 3…) instead of randomly, and compare the time per access over the same 256 MB:

same 256 MB buffer, two access orders · ns per access

sequential
 
0.9 ns
random
96 ns
96 ns

Same data, same size — and sequential is 109× faster. The reason is a piece of hardware called the prefetcher: it watches your memory accesses, notices when you're marching through memory in a steady stride, and races ahead to pull the next chunks into cache before you ask for them. So when your demand arrives, the data's already there. With a predictable pattern the data is effectively always in cache — and the size of the buffer stops mattering at all. With a random pattern the prefetcher is blind and you eat the full memory latency every time.

This is the second recurring idea, the partner to "independence is speed": locality — keeping your accesses close together and predictable. It's often worth more than any cleverness in the algorithm itself.

Chapter 7Branches, and how a CPU "predicts" the future

There's a third way to stall a core: an if. A modern core works on a pipeline — it starts later instructions before earlier ones finish, like an assembly line. But at a branch (if x then … else …) it doesn't yet know which way the program will go, so it can't know which instructions to start next. Its solution is to guess, run ahead down the guessed path, and — if the guess was wrong — throw that work away and restart, a penalty of roughly 15 cycles.

Here's a clean way to see it. Take an array and sum only the elements ≥ 128. Do it once on a sorted array and once on a random one. Same instructions, same amount of data, same memory pattern — the only difference is the order of the values:

summing elements ≥ 128 · cycles per element

sorted
1.5
alternating
1.5
random
4.7
branchless
1.0

The random version is ~3× slower — entirely from wrong guesses. So how does the "guessing" work, and why is sorted so much easier? It's not intelligence. It's a tiny circuit that bets on one dumb fact: branches in real programs are extremely repetitive. The classic design keeps a small counter per branch that essentially means "do what this branch did the last couple of times." On a sorted array the test is false, false, … then true, true, … — one flip the whole way through, trivially predictable. On a random array it's a coin toss the predictor can't beat, so it's wrong about half the time.

Two details make the mechanism obvious. First, the alternating case (true, false, true, false…) is just as fast as sorted — which proves the predictor learns patterns, not just "is it sorted." Only genuine randomness defeats it. Second, if you rewrite the loop to avoid the branch entirely — compute the answer with arithmetic instead of an if (the "branchless" bar) — the data order stops mattering completely. That's both the real-world fix and the proof that the branch was the culprit all along.

Chapter 8SIMD: one instruction, many numbers

Every add in this whole course has handled a single number — that's called scalar work. But there's a second kind of instruction hiding in the chip. A regular register holds one value; a SIMD register (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) is wider — 128 bits on this chip — and you can treat it as several values packed side by side. One SIMD instruction then does the same operation to all of them at once. Picture adding two of these vectors, four numbers each, in a single instruction:

v0 = [ 3 | 8 | 1 | 5 ] v1 = [ 4 | 2 | 9 | 6 ] ───────────────────── one instruction → add all four lanes [ 7 | 10 | 10 | 11 ]

Four adds for the price of one instruction. And it stacks with everything from Chapter 2: the core has several SIMD units, so it can issue several of these per cycle. Two multipliers — lanes inside an instruction, and units across the core. Measured on one core:

integer adds per cycle, one core

scalar
5.9
SIMD (4-wide)
16.6

So one core goes from ~6 to ~17 adds per cycle — a 2.8× jump on top of everything else. (Why 2.8× and not the full 4×? Because scalar was already doing ~6 at once using the regular execution units; there are fewer SIMD units than scalar ones, so the 4-wide lanes net out to ~2.8× rather than 4×.) The same idea applied to floating-point math gives 140 billion floating-point operations per second from a single core.

One thing worth getting straight: a SIMD vector is small — 4 numbers here, up to 16 on some instructions — not thousands. It's a fixed-size register, not a giant array. To process a million numbers you still loop, just chewing 4–16 at a time instead of one. The machine that genuinely does thousands at once is a different beast entirely — the GPU — which we measure in Chapter 12.

Chapter 9The hidden cache: address translation (the TLB)

Programs don't use real memory addresses. Each program sees its own private, pretend "virtual" addresses, and the hardware translates those into real "physical" ones on every single access — a safety and flexibility feature every modern OS relies on. That translation would be ruinously slow to redo each time, so the chip caches the recent translations in a small dedicated table called the TLB. Miss the TLB and the core has to "walk the page tables" — several extra memory lookups just to find where your data lives, before it can even fetch it.

The neat part is you can see this cost completely separate from the data cache. We read the same 128 KB of data two ways: packed tightly (so it spans only a few memory pages, a few translations) versus spread out one item per page (so it spans hundreds of pages, hundreds of translations). The actual data sits in fast L1 cache both times — only the number of address translations differs:

same 128 KB of in-cache data · cycles per access

packed
 
3.8
spread
131
131

30× slower to read the exact same data sitting in the exact same fast cache — purely because the chip ran out of room to remember its addresses. So there are really two caches working on every memory access: one for the data, and this hidden one for the addresses, and you can overwhelm either. (This is also the concrete payoff of a design choice: because Apple uses larger 16 KB memory pages, each TLB entry covers more ground, which is part of how these chips can afford an unusually large L1 cache.)

Chapter 10All the way down: the SSD

Below main memory sits storage — the SSD. It's the bottom of the ladder, and the drop is staggering: a random read takes about 71 microseconds, which at this clock is roughly 315,000 cycles — about 760× slower than DRAM, and 80,000× slower than an L1 hit. But the headline lesson here isn't the raw latency, it's that how you ask matters enormously. Every read from disk is a system call: a round trip from your program down into the operating system and back, with a fixed cost each time.

Watch what happens when we read the same 512 MB file but vary the chunk size we ask for:

reading one 512 MB file, by request size · GB/s

Asking in tiny 4 KB pieces means making that round trip 131,072 times and crawling at 0.1 GB/s; asking in 4 MB gulps means making it 128 times and flying at ~9.7 GB/s — ~100× faster for the identical bytes. It's the same shape as every chapter: a fixed cost only hurts when you fail to amortize it over enough work.

Chapter 11The whole chip, for real

We've measured one core deeply and watched cores scale. The last CPU question is about the two big shared resources — raw compute and memory bandwidth — and the surprise is that they behave completely differently as you add cores. Compute keeps climbing all the way to 18 cores (reaching 1.9 trillion floating-point ops/sec). Memory bandwidth does not:

total memory bandwidth (GB/s) vs threads

One core alone already pulls 104 GB/s — a third of the whole memory system — and by about 6 cores the bandwidth is maxed out at ~300 GB/s. After that, more cores buy nothing, because they're all drinking from one shared pipe. This is the single most practical lesson in the course: whether adding cores helps depends entirely on what your program is limited by. If it's doing math (compute-bound), it scales to all 18 cores. If it's shuffling memory (bandwidth-bound), it saturates around 6 and the rest of the cores are wasted.

Chapter 12The other processor: the GPU

Back in Chapter 8 we said CPU SIMD does a handful of numbers at once, and the "thousands at once" machine is the GPU. Your chip has one built in: a 40-core GPU with roughly 5,000 tiny arithmetic lanes. It reaches 14.9 trillion float ops/sec — about 8× the entire CPU — and 578 GB/s of bandwidth (more than the CPU could pull, which tells us the chip's memory system is even bigger than Chapter 11 showed). But watch what it takes to get there:

GPU compute (TFLOP/s) vs how many threads you give it

Give it only a thousand threads and it manages 1.2 TFLOP/s — slower than the CPU. It doesn't reach full speed until you've handed it hundreds of thousands of threads. That curve is the whole difference between the two processors. A CPU hides waiting with cleverness — the out-of-order execution, branch prediction, and prefetching from earlier chapters all exist to keep a single thread moving — so it's fast even on one thing at a time. A GPU hides waiting with sheer numbers: it has almost none of that cleverness, but so many threads in flight that whenever one stalls on memory, thousands of others are ready to run. Two opposite bets on the same problem (memory is slow) — which is exactly why your machine has both.

In one pictureThe whole machine

We started from the naive model — fetch one instruction, do it, fetch the next — and measured every layer of reality stacked on top of it. Here's the full ladder of where time goes, every rung measured here, with a human-scale column: if one CPU cycle were stretched to one second, how long would each wait feel?

the memory ladder · if one cycle were one second

tierlatencycycles= 1 cyc/sec
registers~0.2 ns~11 second
L1 cache0.9 ns44 seconds
L2 cache~4 ns~2020 seconds
DRAM95 ns4257 minutes
SSD (random)71 µs~315,0003.6 days

A register is now; a trip to main memory is a 7-minute errand; reaching the SSD is like mailing off for the data and waiting almost four days. Everything fast about a computer is the machinery built to keep you near the top of that ladder.

And it all reduces to two knobs, both of which we measured again and again. Independence — is there other work to do while you wait? A chain of dependent steps pins you to 1× no matter the hardware; independent work unlocks ~6–20×. Locality — is your data close and predictable? That's worth up to ~100× between a cache hit and a random trip to DRAM. Multiply them and you span a factor of thousands between the best and worst this same silicon can do. Which end your program lands on is decided mostly by how you arrange your data and your work — not by how many instructions you write. Every clever thing in the chip exists to claw back one of those two gaps, and you can watch each one earn its keep with a stopwatch.

Measured on this machine with timed loops — no spec sheets. "GHz" and "cycles" rest on one assumption (1 dependent add = 1 cycle), corroborated by landing on the known clock. Several figures are best-of-many runs (the hardware's ceiling); real workloads run further from every one. · know-your-machine
